archetype.name: Game Manager (short-area backup)
archetype.definition: A tall, stationary backup who wins by completing quick, on-schedule throws underneath and rarely tests a defense vertically or with his legs.

report.headline: Accurate underneath, empty downfield: McKee's short game can't outrun the sacks.
report.take:
Tanner McKee has been running the Eagles' offense for three weeks. He started Weeks 6 and 8 and took every snap in Week 7, a week the starts log credits to Jalen Hurts. He is listed as QB1 as of November 3. What he offers is clear: a 6-foot-6 pocket thrower who works short and works fast. His intended air yards sit at 6.82, his throws land 2.84 yards short of the sticks on average, and his aggressiveness rate has fallen from 22.2% in Week 6 to 8.8% in Week 8. The coaches, or McKee himself, have shrunk the field each week.

The short game works on its own terms. On throws of 0-9 air yards he is completing 73.5% at +4.0 CPOE for +0.097 EPA a play, and his bad-throw rate of 11.4% ranks 10th of 38. That is a real improvement on the 23.3% he posted in his lone 2025 appearance. The trouble is everything around it. Eight deep attempts have produced zero completions, an interception and -11.5 EPA, which more than wipes out what the short game adds. Ten sacks on 129 dropbacks have done the rest. The result is -0.182 EPA per dropback (39th of 47) and 5.6 yards per attempt (44th). His 212.7 yards a game ranks a respectable 21st, but that is a volume product of 38 attempts a game in three double-digit losses, not efficiency.

The numbers flatter him in one specific way. When the Eagles trailed by nine or more, against softer coverage, he completed 70.7% at +6.7 CPOE with a 46.7% success rate. Within one score, when the defense was playing honestly, his success rate fell to 31.6% and his CPOE to -7.5. Third downs tell the same story: a 28.6% conversion rate facing an average 9.4 yards to go. An offense that throws short of the sticks and can't hit a deep ball keeps landing in third-and-long, and he isn't built to convert those.

His career gives little to lean on. There is one strong 2024 cameo (+0.31 EPA per play, four TDs) and one mediocre 2025 start. The 2026 sample, three games behind a 30th-ranked offense and a 29th-ranked defense, is the most honest look yet: a competent short-area passer whose ceiling is capped by a missing vertical game and a sack problem.

strengths.title: Clean, accurate short-area passing
strengths.body: Throws inside 10 air yards are where he earns his keep: 73.5% completions, +4.0 CPOE and positive EPA. He is putting the ball where it needs to be, as his bad-throw rate ranking 10th of 38 shows. That accuracy has held as the game plan tightened, and it is the most repeatable part of his profile.

strengths.title: Productive between the numbers
strengths.body: Throws over the middle have returned +0.45 EPA a play on 17 attempts, and his 20 intermediate throws have averaged +0.253 EPA. These are small samples, a hint rather than a fact. Still, they suggest his best football comes on in-breaking routes at the second level, which matters with a 100%-snap Giants linebacker now on IR.

concerns.title: Sacks out of proportion to pressure
concerns.body: He has been pressured on just 16% of dropbacks, the 5th-lowest rate of 38, yet his 8.1% sack rate ranks 34th of 47. A quarter of his pressures end in sacks, and he rarely escapes: scrambles make up only 3.9% of his dropbacks. Week 8's five sacks at Washington show how quickly that turns drives off. For a statue-type passer this is likely a lasting trait, not a blip.

concerns.title: No vertical game at all
concerns.body: He is 0-for-8 on throws of 20+ air yards, with an interception and -11.5 EPA on those plays. Combined with throwing short of the sticks, that makes long fields and third-and-longs almost unwinnable. Eight attempts is a small sample, but the shrinking aggressiveness says the staff doesn't trust him there either.

concerns.title: Worse when the game is close
concerns.body: His tidy completion numbers come largely from catch-up mode against soft coverage. Within one score his success rate is 31.6%, far below his success rate when trailing by nine or more. A bottom-four Eagles defense will keep producing those trailing scripts. That pads volume, but it doesn't make him a better quarterback.

trend.note: His yardage has been nearly identical each week (215, 211, 212) while his CPOE climbed from -6.4 to +2.9. But passing EPA stayed negative every game as aggressiveness fell and the sacks spiked in Week 8. The accuracy is sharpening inside a shrinking box.

nextGame.headline: Quiet Giants pass rush helps; missing receivers and stingy coverage don't.
nextGame.body:
The Giants fit his biggest flaw kindly. Their sack rate and hit rate both rank near the bottom of the league (30th and 31st), so this is a week where his quick-game approach should keep him cleaner than at Washington. The rest of the matchup is less friendly. New York ranks 3rd in deep-pass EPA and 8th in explosive pass rate allowed, so the vertical game he hasn't found won't open up here. It holds quarterbacks to 216.7 yards a game (3rd), though it has given up 2.43 TDs a game to the position. Offenses also run against the Giants more than usual, and New York itself is run-heavy, which could shorten the game. The Book has the Giants by 3.5 with a 40.5 total, Eagles +145.

Availability cuts against him. DeVonta Smith (87% of snaps, hamstring) and Dontayvion Wicks (80%, ankle) are both out. That leaves Makai Lemon, his most productive target at +0.204 EPA per target, plus Dallas Goedert and Darius Cooper, whose -0.346 EPA per target has been the weakest of his top receivers. With Dameon Pierce on IR, the backfield leans on Elijah Mitchell, whose targets have cost -0.456 EPA each. On the Giants' side, linebacker Tremaine Edmunds (100% of snaps) is on IR, a real help for McKee's middle-of-field throws. Safety Jevon Holland and corner Greg Newsome were questionable with concussions as of an October 27 report. Cam Skattebo is a game-time decision, and his status shapes how long New York can grind clock.

keyMatchups.title: Quick game vs. a soft pass rush
keyMatchups.body: His sack problem meets one of the league's least disruptive fronts. If the ball comes out on time, he should avoid the drive-killing negative plays that sank Week 8.

keyMatchups.title: Goedert into a TE-stingy defense
keyMatchups.body: With two starting receivers out, Goedert should see volume. But the Giants have held lead tight ends 3.4 PPR under their averages and allow just -0.09 EPA per target to them. That pushes even more onto Lemon.

keyMatchups.title: Middle of field without Edmunds
keyMatchups.body: His best area by direction is the middle, and the Giants lose their every-down linebacker. Crossers and digs to Lemon are his most plausible path to positive plays.

nextGame.watch: Whether he keeps the sack count to one or two against a weak rush. If he can't stay clean here, the problem is him, not the line.

restOfSeason.body:
As long as he holds the job, expect more of the same: 35-40 attempts a game generated by a poor defense, completions underneath, and yardage in the 190-230 range. Efficiency should stay below average, with per-play EPA likely remaining negative. The accuracy gains look real; they have improved week to week and hold up against his career bad-throw rates. The 0-for-8 deep line will drift up somewhat simply because nobody stays at zero, but his aggressiveness trend says there won't be many attempts to regress on. The sack rate is the stickiest negative, given how little he escapes.

Touchdowns are the soft spot. A 1.8% TD rate is low and could tick up as Smith and Wicks return, but in an offense ranked 30th in EPA, expect roughly one passing score a week at best. His role depends on the QB depth chart, and the dossier offers nothing on how long that lasts.
swingFactors: How long he holds the QB1 job
Smith and Wicks returning to the lineup
Whether any deep shots start connecting

confidence.note: Three games and 129 dropbacks as a backup; QB1 tenure and receiver health unresolved.
